references.text: Jesus uses the same image of trees and fruit in the Sermon on the Mount: a good tree bears good fruit, and a bad tree bears bad fruit. "By their fruits you will know them" is the concluding conclusion.
Jesus says directly: "Make the tree good, and its fruit will be good; or make the tree bad, and its fruit will be bad. For by its fruit the tree is known." This is a close parallel to Luke 6:43.

The immediate continuation of Luke 6:43, which expands on the image: every tree is known by its own fruit, and a good person's heart brings forth what is good, while an evil heart brings forth what is evil.
James uses a similar image from nature: a fig tree cannot bear olives, and a vine cannot bear figs. The point is the same: the nature of the source determines what comes out of it.

Isaiah's parable of the vineyard where God expected good fruit from his people but got wild grapes. The image of trees/plants and fruit as an expression of inner character is rooted in Old Testament prophecy.

The Lord says he searches the heart and tests the mind to give each person according to their ways and according to the fruit of their deeds. The connection between the condition of the heart and its fruit is clear.
Paul describes the fruit of the Spirit—love, joy, peace, etc.—as the good fruit that comes from a life led by God's Spirit, in contrast to the works of the flesh (the bad fruit).
John the Baptist urges people to bear fruit worthy of repentance and warns that every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.
